summary: Describes the transport mechanisms for carrying Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) messages: HTTP, file, mail, and TCP. CMC defines the messages for certificate requests and responses, and this document covers how to move them between clients and certificate authorities. It was replaced by RFC 10003.

eli5.summary: If the certificate request is a letter, this explains the ways to deliver it: by web, by file, by email, or by a direct network connection. It has been replaced by RFC 10003.

questions: how to send cmc messages over http
which port does cmc over tcp use
subtitle: Four ways to move CMC certificate request and response messages: files, mail, HTTP and plain TCP.

tldr.problem: CMC defines messages for requesting and issuing certificates, but clients and certificate authorities still need agreed ways to carry those messages between them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four transports: files with fixed extensions, MIME mail, HTTP POST with set content types, and raw TCP with no wrapping.
tldr.outcome: Different environments, from off-line clients to web servers, can exchange CMC messages in an interoperable way. RFC 10003 has replaced this document.

today: RFC 5273 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 10003 and updated by RFC 6402, so use those for current CMC transport rules.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
This document defines transport methods for moving CMC messages (Certificate Management over CMS), which are defined in RFC 5272. The mechanisms are HTTP, file, mail and TCP. It uses the usual RFC 2119 key words such as MUST and SHOULD.

CMC messages come as Simple PKI Requests and Responses, and Full PKI Requests and Responses. The transports differ mostly in how they label and wrap those four message types.
sections.eli5: A certificate request is a letter. This document lists the ways to deliver the letter, and how to write on the envelope so the receiver knows what is inside.

sections.title: File and Mail Transports
sections.content:
With the file-based transport, requests and responses move by file-system means, for example when enrollment is done for an off-line client. There MUST be only one request or response message in a single file. File extensions SHOULD be .p10 (Simple PKI Request), .crq (Full PKI Request), .p7c (Simple PKI Response) and .crp (Full PKI Response).

The mail-based transport uses MIME wrapping, taken from S/MIME. MIME wrapping between the layers of CMS wrapping is optional, which differs from a standard S/MIME message. A simple request uses content type application/pkcs10 with a .p10 file name. The other three message types use application/pkcs7-mime with an smime-type parameter and a file name that MUST be included in the content-type or content-disposition statement.
sections.eli5: On a disk you put one message per file and end the file name with a code that says what kind it is. In email you stick a label on the attachment that says the same thing.

sections.title: HTTP and TCP Transports
sections.content:
For HTTP, clients MUST use the POST method to submit requests and servers MUST use the 200 response code for successful responses. The Content-Type header MUST carry the right value from the MIME table, and the body is the binary encoding of the PKI Request or PKI Response (a BER encoding for responses). Clients MAY try TLS 1.0 or later, although servers are not required to support TLS. Servers MUST NOT assume client support for any HTTP authentication such as cookies, Basic or Digest.

For TCP, no wrapping is required: messages are sent in their binary encoded form. The client closes the connection after the response or sends another request on it, and reusing one connection for successive requests is RECOMMENDED. A server MAY close an idle connection, typically after several minutes. No specific port is assigned. Only the Private Ports 49152-65535 may be used without registration, ports 1-49151 SHOULD NOT be used, and the port is configured out of band.
sections.eli5: On the web, you post the request like a form and get the answer back. With plain TCP you just send the bytes down a pipe, and both sides agree on the door number beforehand.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Replay attacks may need to be thwarted depending on the operating environment. If the CA keeps significant state, replays may be detectable without the optional nonces. Implementers need to weigh whether to use the senderNonce and recipientNonce attributes, and developers of state-constrained PKI clients are strongly encouraged to use them.

Setting up a secure channel between an end-entity and a CA or RA requires an out-of-band trust initiation mechanism, for example IPsec or TLS, and the choice is outside the scope of this document. When no prior trust exists, such as when the protocol downloads the trust anchors, the Enveloped Data content type must be used to give the shrouding TLS would have provided.
sections.eli5: Someone could copy an old message and send it again, so some systems add one-time numbers. And you need some way to trust who you are talking to before you start.
